title: Parle-G's "Bharat Ka Apna Biscuit" Campaign: When a Biscuit Becomes a Chronicle of National Pride - MarkHub24
content: In 1938, a biscuit was born. It wasn't designed to be luxurious or trendy. It was designed to be affordable, accessible, nourishing. It was designed to reach into modest Indian homes and become part of daily life. Over nearly 80 years, as India transformed—from a nation under colonial rule to a free republic, from an agrarian economy to a technological superpower—Parle-G remained constant. It was there during India's struggles. It was there during India's triumphs. It witnessed and nourished generations of Indians who would shape the nation's destiny. In January 2017, on the occasion of India's 73rd Republic Day, Parle-G launched a campaign called "Bharat Ka Apna Biscuit" (India's Own Biscuit). The campaign wasn't primarily about the biscuit's taste or nutritional value. It was about something far larger: the intimate, inseparable bond between a humble product and an entire nation's journey. The campaign positioned Parle-G not just as a brand, but as a witness to, and participant in, India's evolution. Featuring actor Piyush Mishra and music composed by legendary lyricist Javed Akhtar, the campaign created something rare in commercial advertising: a meditation on national identity, homegrown pride, and the profound truth that India's progress has been built on the contributions of millions of ordinary people nourishing themselves on extraordinary ambitions. What makes the "Bharat Ka Apna Biscuit" campaign strategically brilliant is the insight from which it emerges. Mayank Shah, Category Head at Parle Products, articulated this insight with clarity: "We at Parle are proud of the achievements and milestones of young Indians. Whether it is in science, technology, fashion or sports, Indians today are making a difference in the world." But more fundamentally, the campaign was saying something about what Parle-G represents: not an imported luxury, not a Western product adapted for Indian markets, but India's own creation. A biscuit made by Indians, for Indians, that has nourished India's progress for nearly eight decades. This positioning tapped into something profound that was emerging in Indian consciousness by 2017: a reaffirmation of pride in homegrown products, a questioning of the idea that global always means better, and a recognition that India's strength comes from its own people, its own innovations, its own values. The campaign also recognized that nationalism doesn't have to be aggressive or exclusionary. It can be about quiet pride. It can be about acknowledging that ordinary products—a biscuit, for instance—can carry extraordinary meaning when they're connected to a nation's journey. The 30-second TVC was deceptively simple. Rather than elaborate production or multiple scenarios, the campaign focused on a single, powerful narrative device: music. Javed Akhtar's lyrics, set to composition, told the story of Parle-G's journey with India. The lyrics spoke of how, since 1938, Parle-G had been "making biscuits that have nurtured geniuses in many Indian households" and given them "the energy to make history with each passing..." The language was poetic yet accessible. It didn't claim Parle-G made people geniuses. It claimed Parle-G nurtured them—supported them, sustained them, accompanied them on their journeys. By using Javed Akhtar—arguably India's most respected lyricist, known for politically conscious, socially aware songwriting—Parle-G was making a statement about artistic credibility. This wasn't a commercial jingle. This was literature. This was poetry. This was a nationally significant artist lending his voice to celebrate an Indian product's connection to the nation. Piyush Mishra's narration added another layer. Mishra is known for his ability to convey depth and sincerity through subtle performance. His presence in the campaign communicated that this wasn't fluff. This was something worth taking seriously—a brand's genuine relationship with a nation. The creative direction from Samir Chonkar of Everest Brand Solutions shows the hand of someone who understood that sometimes less is more. Rather than showing scenes of Indians achieving things (which could have felt clichéd), the campaign simply spoke poetically about this relationship, trusting audiences to understand the implicit message. The "Bharat Ka Apna Biscuit" campaign was explicitly positioned as the evolution of Parle-G's famous previous campaign: "Roko Mat Toko Mat" (Don't Stop, Taste It). The creative team acknowledged this heritage while showing how the brand's positioning could evolve for a new moment—from celebration of the product's taste to celebration of the product's role in India's national journey. This continuation was strategic for several reasons. First, it tapped into nostalgia for audiences who had grown up with Parle-G and remembered "Roko Mat Toko Mat." Second, it positioned Parle-G as a brand that evolves without abandoning its essence. And third, it suggested that the brand's contribution to India has always been about more than just feeding people—it's been about sustaining India's aspirations. The campaign positioned Parle-G as part of India's national story without being preachy or obvious. For marketers and business students, this teaches that the most powerful brand-nation alignment often comes from suggesting the connection poetically rather than stating it directly. By speaking of nurturing geniuses and making history, Parle-G created space for audiences to understand the deeper meaning without being lectured. Parle-G's 79-year history became its greatest asset. By positioning the brand as a witness to India's journey, Parle-G claimed authenticity that no competitor could match. For business students, this demonstrates that heritage isn't just nostalgic. It's a strategic asset that can justify premium positioning and emotional connection. By commissioning Javed Akhtar and casting Piyush Mishra, Parle-G elevated commercial messaging into something that felt like art. For marketers, this teaches that sometimes the most powerful way to make audiences take your brand seriously is to treat the advertising itself seriously—not as commercial manipulation, but as cultural expression. Rather than attacking imported brands or claiming superiority through comparison, the campaign simply celebrated Indians and Indian achievement. For business students, this demonstrates that the most sustainable patriotic positioning comes from affirming rather than attacking, from building up rather than tearing down. The campaign explicitly positioned itself as evolution of "Roko Mat Toko Mat," not replacement. For marketers, this teaches that the most powerful repositioning often comes from respecting what came before while extending it into new territory. This creates continuity and makes audiences feel like they're watching a brand grow alongside them. What emerges from the "Bharat Ka Apna Biscuit" campaign is Parle-G positioning itself not as a company selling products, but as a national institution—a brand that has participated in India's journey, nurtured its people, and contributed to its progress. This positioning allowed Parle-G to command premium respect despite competing in a commodity category dominated by global players. It positioned the brand not primarily on taste or price, but on meaning and belonging. What makes Parle-G's "Bharat Ka Apna Biscuit" campaign remarkable is that it accomplishes something rare in commercial advertising: it transforms a product into a historical chronicle, commerce into culture, and a biscuit into a symbol of national pride. For marketers and business students analyzing this campaign, the central lesson is this: the most powerful brand positioning often comes from understanding your product's authentic role in consumers' lives and in national narratives, then communicating that role poetically rather than commercially. When Parle-G positioned itself as having nurtured generations of Indians and supported their achievements, it positioned itself as essential not to consumption, but to identity. In the lyrics composed by Javed Akhtar, in Piyush Mishra's sincere narration, in the simple, powerful message that a humble biscuit has been part of India's greatest journey—in all of that, Parle-G created advertising that transcends commerce. It created something that feels like national documentation, like cultural history, like acknowledgment of a bond that has endured through decades of transformation. That is not just good advertising. That is cultural leadership. That is the power of understanding that sometimes the most humble products carry the most profound meanings.

title: Karol G's new album may just have you crying at the club - AOL.com
content: It may be summertime, but Karol G is unapologetically leaning into her sadness. On Friday, the Colombian pop star released her seventh studio album “No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto,” a 14-track project that details the depths of heartache one can only access when finally tuning out the world. Tinged with dream-pop accents and acoustic instrumentation — though still fringed with her signature reggaeton-pop flair — it is a dramatic departure from her previous album, “Tropicoqueta,” a lofty, genre-rich album that envisioned a Latina-led utopia as a tropic floral paradise. Now, with “No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto” — which in English translates to “I Don’t Regret Feeling So Much” — Karol G swaps her vibrant, tropical facade for a soft blue vulnerability. Her special new brand of perreo melancolía features guest vocals by Drake (who sings in Spanish), Bruno Mars, Greg Gonzalez (of Cigarettes After Sex), as well as Spanish stars Judeline and Rusowsky. The melodrama begins early on with the opening track, “Te Llevas To” — a moody EDM elegy that explores the loss of one’s self after a relationship ends. In an interview with Elle magazine, the hit maker shared that she spent a lot of time alone when creating this project, following her split from Colombian singer-songwriter Feid late last year — long before headlines caught wind of their breakup in January. “Everything started when I went to Hawaii [last November]. I did a lot of hiking alone. I would climb the mountains alone. I would stand there gazing at the sky. I learned a lot about enjoying my solitude in this industry — we are really, really lonely. Compared to the rest of the world, you’re very isolated,” said Karol G in  the Elle interview. Rumblings of the new project first surfaced in April when Karol G performed at the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival as its first Latina headliner. There, she debuted “Después de Ti,” a shoegaze ballad joined by Greg Gonzalez, frontman of the indie-pop band Cigarettes After Sex; the song expressed profound grief after Karol experienced a loved one’s  death. “I cry a lot. I’m super sentimental and I’ve hated myself a lot for that,” Karol G revealed to Elle in her July cover story. “But at the same time, I’d rather suffer because I lived too much — because I loved too much, because I had too much fun — than to not have had those experiences, you know? I’m inviting everyone to be a little more dramatic, a little more extra.” Although her classic bichota essence — a term Karol G frequently uses to describe herself, as a female counterpart to the Puerto Rican bichote, or “big shot” — is still heavily present in the new LP. Earlier this summer, Karol teased the song “Matadora” during the opening night of her international stadium tour in Chicago; produced by reggaeton pioneer Tainy, the sultry track  is hallmarked by a muffled jazz trumpet and suggestive verses for an unknown paramour. Her longtime collaborator, Colombian record producer Ovy On The Drums, also returns to incorporate elements of Karol’s the Grammy-winning 2023 album, “Mañana Será Bonito,” which followed her public breakup with ex-fiancé Anuel AA and grew into a massive commercial hit. With Ovy, Karol revived the shadowy timbre of her joint Shakira track “TQG” into the new “Bebiendo Lágrimas,” a reggaeton song that adamantly rejects the notion of love. Mexican American producer Edgar Barrera — who previously worked with Karol on her merengue smash “Si Antes Te Hubiera Conocido,” as well as “Mi Ex Tenía Razón” and “Gucci los Paños” — reprises his role as a música mexicana connoisseur, aiding in Karol’s synth-doused Tejana-style cumbia, “Alguien Que Te Amaba.” (The track was also written with legendary songwriter Pete Astudillo, who co-wrote many of Selena Quintanilla‘s greatest hits.) In the anguished “Con Quien Andara,” the singer pays tribute to the Spanish singer-songwriter Jeanette and her hazy, sentimental pop ballad from 1976 titled “Porque Te Vas?” And if that’s not enough of a nostalgia bomb, there’s the dream-pop reggaeton track “Bby Wow,” which features Judeline and Rusowsky and was inspired by the popular 2003 dancehall track, “Coolie Dance Rhythm” by Cordel “Scatta” Burrell. (Millennials may also recall echoes of this sample in popular tracks like Nina Sky and Jabba’s 2004 “Move Ya Body.”) A word of advice for the Karol G fans — tropicoquetas and bichotas alike — this is an intimate record that’s best heard alone for the first time. So light up that candle, lock the doors and bring the tissues if you have to — just don’t be ashamed to feel all the feels, or shake your booty if the mood strikes. title: BMW F 450 GS Performance Tested and Explained - Autocar India
content: The BMW F 450 GS line-up is spread across three variants – Base, Exclusive and GS Trophy – which share the same engine and differ based on features and components. The 420cc parallel-twin liquid-cooled engine produces 48hp at 8,750rpm and 43Nm at 6,750rpm, paired with a 6-speed gearbox. BMW’s Shift Assistant Pro for clutchless upshifts and downshifts is standard from the Exclusive variant. For this test, we had the top-spec variant that gets BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch. For the acceleration test, we were riding the bike in Road mode with the traction control turned off. We launched the bike manually instead of using the Easy Ride Clutch for a quick launch off the line. The bike offers potent performance in the mid range and acceleration tapers off as the revs climb close to the redline. The F 450 GS achieved the 0-100kph sprint in 5.72 seconds, which is a quick timing. In our roll-on acceleration tests, the bike took 1.81 seconds to get from 20-50kph, 3.04 seconds from 30-70kph, and 2.95 seconds for the 50-80kph run. In the city, it is tractable, able to make quick overtakes effortlessly and the Easy Ride Clutch makes commutes with a lot of traffic a breeze. The F 450 GS features disc brakes at both ends with dual channel ABS. The feedback at the lever is sharp and in our tests, it took just 16.52 metres to come to a complete stop from 60kph. The tyres are also really grippy and inspired confidence, despite the road being wet. The bike is priced starting at Rs 4.70 lakh for the Base, Rs 4.90 lakh for the Exclusive, and goes up to Rs 5.30 lakh for the GS Trophy variant (ex-showroom prices).

title: Vikings Training Camp Observations: Jamal Adams Switches Jersey & Roles - Minnesota Vikings
content: EAGAN, Minn. — An early afternoon thunderstorm preceded a gorgeous afternoon of football Friday at TCO Performance Center as the Vikings picked back up in full pads after a day off. In case you've lost track of the 2026 Training Camp action, Minnesota will be headed to New Jersey a week from now to prepare for its preseason opener at the New York Giants on Saturday, Aug. 15. As far as the ongoing quarterback competition between Kyler Murray, who turned 29 today, and J.J. McCarthy, both players made a couple difficult throws in a session heavy with specific game situations, and they had a couple more fall incomplete by the skin of their teeth. Two stuck with us: Murray laid one up the seam to TE Ben Yurosek that almost resulted in a diving catch, and McCarthy arced one up the sideline to TE Gavin Bartholomew that looked grabbable — granted, it would've been a head-turner. On the defensive side, Dallas Turner, Andrew Van Ginkel and Blake Cashman supplied some of the most notable pressure on the passers, and Jalen Redmond played with ownership of the trenches. Here are three observations from practice No. 8, which was officiated by NFL referees: View photos of Vikings players during Training Camp practice on August 7. We got our first long look this summer at All-Pro kicker Will Reichard, and he looked as advertised. During an extended period (nearly 20 minutes), the offense worked third- and fourth-down calls, and depending on the result either finished the sequence by sending out the field goal/punting units or leaving the offense on the field to convert. Ultimately, Reichard was tasked with five FG attempts. The 25-year-old drilled his initial try from 57 yards and then narrowly missed his second from 58 yards, which hit the crossbar. He responded with makes from 46, 43 and 48 yards to finish 4-for-5. As well as he performed, it's not outlandish to say rookie punter Brett Thorson stole the show. Thorson followed veteran Johnny Hekker, who punted twice (one of Hekker's was downed at the 20-yard line, the other bounced through the back of the end zone), and placed his first ball at the 1-yard line (Tai Felton gunned down the field and missed a chance to down it before it rolled into the end zone). Afterward, in a separate special teams period, Thorson took all the punter reps and compiled his own highlight reel, smashing ball after ball to smithereens. We couldn't get a perfect read on the distances but are comfortable saying several traveled 60 yards. The returners were in retreat mode. It was a fun introduction for fans to the Australian punter and the Ray Guy Award winner at Georgia. Jamal Adams sported a new number, 32, after donning 54 in his first seven Vikings practices. The 30-year-old defender probably feels a little bit more at home in it after rocking 33 on the Jets and Seahawks (and Titans and Raiders). Adams likely also felt more himself as he moved all around Minnesota's defense. Adams is listed as a linebacker on the roster and was just that to begin his Vikings tenure, playing alongside the likes of Blake Cashman, Eric Wilson and Ivan Pace, Jr. On Friday, however, Adams got more exposure to Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores' creativity and played in the box, over the slot and as one of two deep safeties next to Joshua Metellus. It's worth noting that safety Jay Ward did not practice, and rookie Jakobe Thomas did not participate in team drills. Nevertheless, it was neat to see Adams patrolling several areas. Due to Adams changing his number, OLB Chaz Chambliss switched to 57, which he wore in 2025. View photos of the Vikings roster as of Aug. 7, 2026. There were a few occasions Friday of past-and-present teammates victimizing each other. During a 7-on-7 period, cornerback Byron Murphy, Jr., jumped a route by Justin Jefferson and intercepted Murray, his 2019 draft classmate on the Cardinals. Murph' stuck like glue to "Jets", again, in 11-on-11 and drew a pass interference penalty when Jefferson attempted to push off him. The offense reached into its bag of tricks in the red zone versus a scout defense to wrap practice — and this time, there was a triple Big Blue connection that favored McCarthy and Max Bredeson. On one snap, Bredeson took his fullback stance and spearheaded a touchdown rush by Aaron Jones, Sr., with a sledgehammer block that would make C.J. Ham proud on former Michigan LB Josh Ross; they go back to Bredeson's freshman season, when Ross led the Wolverines with 106 tackles! On the very next snap, McCarthy found his college buddy in the flat for an easy pitch-and-catch TD. title: Karol G’s New Album Rejects the Idea That Healing Is Linear - HipLatina
content:
Credit: Evan Agostini/Invision/AP | Associated Press There is a long history of Latina women being allowed to feel deeply in music—but not necessarily in real life. There are the ballads. The boleros. The rancheras. It’s why all it takes to get a group of Latinas deep in their feelings is to put them in a room with some alcohol and play songs by Juan Gabriel, Ana Gabriel, Marco Antonio Solís, or La India. In Mexico, there are even bars called salas de despecho where people go to do exactly that: let out their grief and feelings by singing along to heartbreak songs. Karol G, who released her seventh studio album today, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, is a big fan of salas de despecho. I know because I stood just feet away from her at one in San Miguel, Mexico, last fall, watching her sing along to those heartbreak songs with such conviction you’d think she was actually grieving a breakup herself. As it turns out, she was. The world didn’t catch on until January, but by then the Colombian pop star had already split from her boyfriend, Feid. Her new album isn’t simply about heartbreak. It’s about what happens when a woman allows herself actually to feel her feelings—to sit with them, move through them, and resist the pressure to heal quickly, move on, and turn her pain into a lesson. Karol’s album embraces the full range of emotions that surfaced after her breakup in real time. She didn’t wait years to look back and reflect on the experience. Instead, she spent time alone unpacking, processing, and crying through it. You feel that immediately when the album begins with the opening track “Te Llevas To,” a song about losing pieces of yourself after heartbreak. “I cry a lot. I’m super sentimental, and I’ve hated myself a lot for that,” Karol said in a recent interview with ELLE about the album. “But at the same time, I’d rather suffer because I lived too much—because I loved too much, because I had too much fun—than not to have had those experiences, you know? I’m inviting everyone to be a little more dramatic,  a little more extra.” That is the foundation holding this album together: permission to grieve a loss. We talk about heartbreak today as if it’s supposed to follow a formula. You fall in love. You experience a breakup and the pain of losing someone. You feel sadness. Then you go to therapy, heal quickly, and emerge with your empowering glow-up. While that might be how grief is packaged on our social media feeds, it’s rarely how it actually works. Grief is not linear. You can have a great day and wake up the next morning feeling completely devastated all over again. You can acknowledge that someone wasn’t right for you and still miss them terribly. And you can be a star as massive as Karol G and still feel incredibly lonely. “Everything started when I went to Hawaii [last November]. I did a lot of hiking alone. I would climb the mountains alone. I would stand there gazing at the sky,” she told ELLE. “I learned a lot about enjoying my solitude in this industry—we are really, really lonely. Compared to the rest of the world, you’re very isolated.” That’s why the title of this album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, which translates to “I Don’t Regret Feeling Deeply,” is so powerful. She’s not simply saying she’s sensitive. She’s rejecting the cultural expectation that feeling emotional pain is a failure—or a weakness—and saying it’s OK to sit with what you’re feeling. Women are constantly advised that after a breakup, they need to focus on healing, moving on, growing, becoming stronger, learning the lesson, and eventually finding someone better. But on this album, Karol G seems to be asking: What if I don’t need to turn my pain into a lesson just yet? What if I can give myself time and room to feel it? The album, which moves away from the tropical reggaetón-pop sound that has defined much of Karol G’s work, is filled with moodier pop ballads and unexpected genre shifts—from “Con Quién Andará,” which pays tribute to Spanish singer and songwriter Jeanette’s 1976 song “Porque Te Vas,” to the Mexican-style cumbia track “Alguien Que Te Amaba,” produced by Mexican American producer Edgar Barrera and co-written by legendary songwriter Pete Astudillo, who co-wrote many of Selena Quintanilla’s greatest hits. In many ways, this album feels like Karol translating her own heartbreak—and the traditional ritual of the sala de despecho, which we know she embraces—into her songwriting. Because when you think about it, a sala de despecho isn’t really about getting over someone. The term itself translates to “heartbreak room.” When we sing throwback songs like Ana Gabriel’s “Quién Como Tú,” it’s not because we’re trying to move past the pain. It’s because we’re permitting ourselves to sit in it—to be devastated for a few hours, to sing it out loud, and to experience the emotional release that comes with it. In many ways, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto feels like the album you make after spending a night at a sala de despecho. What’s interesting is that at no point does Karol hint at the idea of actually moving on from heartbreak. The album doesn’t close with a happy ending. Instead, it ends with “Después de Ti,” which was released in April and debuted at this year’s Coachella. The deeply moving track explores the disorientation and emptiness that can follow a loss. Interestingly, the song was written with Greg Gonzalez of Cigarettes After Sex—a band Karol revealed in a recent Rolling Stone interview that she listened to extensively following her breakup. It’s also telling that she chose to debut this song at Coachella during the same year she became the festival’s first Latina headliner. A deeply emotional song about grief came into existence during one of the most significant moments of her career. There’s something incredibly poetic about that. Karol’s performance demonstrated that she can be at the peak of her career while still making space for heartbreak and grief. And that’s powerful because it reflects the reality of adulthood: You can be winning in life and devastated at the same time. You can be Karol G—celebrated and loved by millions—and still feel lonely, sad, and isolated in private moments. I actually found “Still” with Bruno Mars to be one of the most powerful songs on the album precisely because it is the only English-language track. At first, it comes across as the album’s obvious crossover moment, but once you sit with the lyrics, you realize it’s something much deeper. The song is about continuing to love someone even after they’re gone—holding onto that love even with a heart that’s been broken. Meanwhile, “Ahí” featuring Drake—which, by the way, features him singing in Spanish once again—is about something entirely different: giving yourself the time and space to recover after you’ve finally moved on, even if you aren’t quite ready to open your heart to someone new. There’s a reason Mañana Será Bonito was such a major success: Karol does some of her most intimate work when she taps into the person underneath Karol G the superstar. This album made me think about the emotional whiplash she must experience as one of the biggest Latina music artists in the world—performing for thousands of people, being celebrated globally, and then going home to realize she’s still a person who has to sit with heartbreak. I personally loved Tropicoqueta—despite the criticism it received. It was such a vibrant and celebratory album, and one that Latinas frankly needed amid the attacks and hostility targeting Latine communities in the U.S. this past year. But her latest album feels much more intimate because it isn’t just about Karol G the artist—it’s about what Carolina Giraldo Navarro the person has been feeling since her breakup last fall. You could argue that Karol does some of her best work when she gives herself the space to feel. This is where we get to witness her artistic progression in how willing she is to let audiences experience the full range of her humanity. As women—and especially as Latinas—we’re constantly discouraged from “feeling too much.” I couldn’t relate to that more. Feeling deeply is something women are often taught to correct, minimize, or apologize for. For centuries, women’s emotions have been dismissed and demonized under patriarchy. But with this album, Karol G pushes back against that idea, encouraging her fans and listeners to embrace whatever feelings arise instead of rushing to suppress them. In my opinion, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto is not a breakup album. It’s about what emerges when we refuse to apologize for the heavy emotions, contradictions, and messiness that come after heartbreak. It’s about rejecting the pressure to turn pain into a redemption story. After listening to this album, I’m not even convinced Karol has fully healed—and I don’t think she needs to be. title: Drake Appears on Karol G’s New Album. Let’s Look at His Past Latin Music Collaborations - Rolling Stone
content: It’s official, Drake and Karol have collaborated on new song “Ahí” from the Colombian superstar’s latest release No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto. The sultry track features Champagne Papi at his best. “Drake singing in Spanish has always been incredible to me,” Karol recently told Rolling Stone. “We started talking about making it a duet, like the verses responding to each other. And I was like, ‘I don’t know, but I’d love it if Drake sang it in Spanish.” The collab comes after months of rumors that the pair had worked on music together. In May, Charlamagne tha God added to that frenzy when he claimed that Karol G appearance on Iceman, Drake’s latest release. As it turns out, those rumors were based on a leaked version of the track. Either way, a Karol G collaboration makes perfect sense given Drake’s history of collaborating with Latin music artists. Over the course of his career, Drake has often embodied his Champagne Papi persona and dabbled with Latin music, working with some of the genre’s biggest stars. He’s hopped on tracks for Romeo Santos, Bad Bunny, and rising música mexicana artist Chino Pacas, and even tapped these artists for his own songs. Below, we look back at all of the times the rap superstar expanded the boundaries of his sound to include Latin music. On 2011 hit “The Motto,” Drake famously sang about how “Spanish girls love [him] like [he’s] Aventura.” Three years later, life imitated art when the rapper hopped on a song with Romeo Santos, lead singer of the New York bachata group he name-checked. The melancholic, bachata-flavored track is Drake’s first-ever attempt at singing in Spanish, and he gives it his best: “Celo sus besos / Sobre tu cuerpo / La envidia se apodera así de mí,” he sings, which translates to “I’m jealous of kisses / On your body / Envy takes hold of me.” It’s proof that even in another language, the moody rapper still can’t shake his loverlorn disposition. In 2018, Bad Bunny and Drake teamed up for a collaboration that shifted the conversation between hip-hop and Latin trap. The song perfectly fused signature elements from both genres, creating a club hit that peaked at Number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and gave Bad Bunny, a then-rising star, his first top ten on the chart as a lead artist. “Mía,” which was featured on the the Puerto Rican musician’s debut LP X 100pre, also marked the first time Drake rapped entirely in Spanish for a song, which Bad Bunny insisted on. “It was a great moment for both [of us],” Benito told Billboard Canada recently. “He really believed in Latin music at that time. It was the very beginning.” Five years later, Drake tapped Bad Bunny for a track on his For All the Dogs LP. This time the Canadian rapper went into Spanish-accented Drizzy mode but only for a couple of lines before continuing to spit over a classic dembow beat. True to his roots, Bad Bunny delivered his verses in Spanish with a uniquely Boricua flow. “Gently” didn’t come with a music video filmed in Miami like “Mía” did, but it still charted at Number 12 on the Hot 100. Drake and Gordo have been longtime collaborators; Gordo is known for a bunch of tracks on Drake’s 2022 album Honestly, Nevermind. So it made sense that in 2024, Drake hopped on artist/DJ/producer Gordo’s third LP Diamantes, working as an unofficial consultant on the entire album. “He rides for me that heavy and he’s letting the world know that,” Gordo told Rolling Stone at the time. On both “Healing” and “Sideways,” Drake sings about love lost, his R&B-inflected vocals contrasting Gordo’s electronic beats for a hypnotic effect. Drake further explored the world of Latin music when he worked with música mexicana artist Chino Pacas on a corrido. The Toronto rapper sings “Cubanas me gusta portarlas, dinero es poder” over a flurry of guitarrón, accordion, and saxophone notes. “Modo Capone” came together after Drake saw Pacas perform at the Houston Rodeo. Later, he hit up the música mexicana artist over Instagram DM, asking him to write a song for him. Pacas sent him “3 Letras (OVO),” a corrido dedicated to the rapper’s success. It was impressive enough that Drake hopped on a song with Pacas, gifting the young artist with a major collaboration for his debut LP. “You can tell his professionalism and his years in the industry,” Pacas told Rolling Stone at the time. “It’s something else. We have a lot of chemistry and that’s why we ended up working together.” The chemistry between Pacas and Drake remained strong a few months later when Pacas jumped on Drake and PartyNextDoor’s joint album $ome $exy $ongs 4 U for “Meet Your Padre.” The track is heavy on the Toronto influence, filtering any Mexican notes through an icy OVO sheen as Pacas delivers lines in Spanish with his signature throaty timbre. Meanwhile, Drake sticks to English and briefly confuses his Latin references, rapping about a Brazilian city, the Dominican genre “bachata,” and Mexican girls in the same verse. Drake’s latest Spanish-language collab has been a long time coming. In the lead-up to the rapper’s highly anticipated album, speculation about the project reached a fever pitch when rumors swirled that Karol G was going to appear on the record after “a little bit of the song leaked,” according to the Colombian superstar. “Ahí” interpolates a bit of Drake’s “New Bestie” from Maid of Honor in the last verse, where he name drops Karol G in English. But mostly, it’s a Champagne Papi moment as Drake sings about courting the singer in Spanish. “I guided him through the recording so I could help him with the pronunciation,” Karol G told RS. “The pronunciation was super important to him, and he was constantly like, ‘Please, I have to get the pronunciation down.'” We want to hear it. title: Karol G Turns Heartbreak Into a Superstar Moment on No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto: Review - consequence.net
content: Log in to track artists, discover shows, and stay in the loop. On her new album, the Colombian pop star turns heartbreak into a deeply personal and genre-defying work, embracing the creative freedom that comes with her status as a global superstar The exact moment Karol G became a global superstar is up for debate. Some people place it somewhere around her historic Coachella set in April, in which she became the festival’s first Latina headliner. Others can probably point to the announcement of her “Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour” that kicked off July 24th in Chicago and will see her perform, as only superstars do, in stadiums around the world. Regardless of when it happened, there’s little doubt that Karol G is now part of that exclusive club. And her new album No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto reflects the kind of creative freedom reserved for artists who’ve reached that level. A ballad performed entirely in English? Sure. A Drake-esque track featuring Drake himself? Why not? A gut-wrenching duet going toe to toe with Bruno Mars on vocals? Absolutely. But the album’s greatest strength has little to do with the guest list or the language. No Me Arrepiento is, above all, Karol G’s version of a concept album, one stitched together by heartbreak from beginning to end, with a few pauses here and there to make room for the kind of reggaeton bangers and dance tracks that have made her one of the genre’s defining stars. Funny thing about heartbreak: it makes for some amazing music. Especially when performed by women. Albums like Alanis Morissette’s Jagged Little Pill and Adele’s 21 received universal praise not only for their musical merits but for the catharsis they found in breakups and relationships gone awry. Just last year Lily Allen returned from a seven-year hiatus with West End Girl, a streaming and critical success that explored her separation from actor David Harbour. No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto falls squarely into this rich tradition. Great breakup albums don’t just invite repeated listens. They invite investigation. Fans become detectives, searching for that fine line that separates confession from fiction. Alanis had Dave Coulier. Karol G leaves just enough breadcrumbs to point toward the mystery man behind her heartbreak… But more on that in a minute. Like many of these albums, No Me Arrepiento’s opening track, titled “Te Llevas To,” serves as a mission statement for everything that follows, introducing every emotional theme Karol G spends the next 43 minutes unraveling. The song itself spends most of its runtime swinging back and forth between longing (“I hold on to who I was, to all the times we made love”) and blame (“You can take everything—except my dignity”) before ditching metaphors altogether in favor of a profanity-laden cry that signals the end of her patience: “Hijueputa cabrón, hijueputa cabrón” (which loosely translates to “fucking asshole”). From then on the album evolves into an exploration of the emotional stages of a breakup. There’s the attempt to bury the pain in “Bebiendo Lágrimas,” reluctant acceptance in “Maybe” and “Alguien que te amaba,” jealousy in “¿Con quién andará?,” and the illusion of healing in “Si lo ven.” The lyrics are at times contradictory, shifting sharply between nostalgia and resentment from one song to another. Then again, so is getting over someone you love. Musically, No Me Arrepiento reflects the same emotional rollercoaster. La Bichota moves effortlessly from stripped-back ballads to glossy R&B, atmospheric alt-pop, acoustic confessionals and, whenever the weight threatens to become too much, some good old-fashioned perreo, as is the case with the raunchy “Matadora”, a throwback to old-school reggaeton. In contrast to last year’s Tropicoqueta, her newest effort seems less intent on delivering the next reggaeton anthem than on showcasing her range as a performer, with her voice taking center stage much more often than in previous records. Vulnerable at times, defiant in others, her vocal delivery complements the album’s overarching concept perfectly. Inviting guest artists onto such an intimate album could have been a risky proposition. However, Drake, Bruno Mars and Spanish experimental pop artist rusowsky elevate three of the album’s standout tracks, each knowing exactly when to step forward and when to let Karol G’s story remain at the center. No Me Arrepiento has sparked a scavenger hunt among fans eager to find clues as to who the man referenced in the lyrics might be. Most easter eggs, however, point to reggaeton artist Feid, who dated La Bichota for three years before the pair called it quits earlier this year. The main piece of evidence can be found on “Alguien que te amaba”, the seventh track on the album, which mentions “verano rosa” (pink summer) the title of a collaboration between the two from 2025’s Tropicoqueta album. The twist? The lyric claims that “the pink summer is now winter.” Regardless of the rumors, Karol G seems to have reached a new artistic level with No Me Arrepiento, delivering an album that feels both deeply personal and profoundly universal. If this is what she can do with heartbreak, it’s hard not to be excited about what she’ll do next. title: Karol G's unexpected collab with Bruno Mars is deeply moving: Listen here their new song 'Still' - HOLA
content: Karol G is entering a new chapter with one of her most unexpected collaborations to date. On her newly released album No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto, the Colombian superstar joins forces with Bruno Mars for the emotional ballad "Still," marking a major milestone in her career. The track is especially significant because Karol G sings entirely in English. Paired with Bruno Mars' soulful vocals, "Still" delivers a heartfelt exploration of love, heartbreak, and lingering emotions that stands apart from the Latin star's signature reggaeton and pop hits. Fans have watched Karol G evolve from reggaeton chart-topper to one of the biggest global names in Latin music. While she has previously incorporated English phrases into songs, "Still" is her first collaboration performed completely in English as part of her album. In 2021 she collaborated on "Don't Be Shy" with Tiësto. This one is considered Karol G's first English-language song, although it's a Tiësto single featuring her, she sings entirely in English. Now the difference with "Still" featuring Bruno Mars, is that this is her first full English-language song on one of her own albums, No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto. This move also highlights her growing international reach while staying true to the emotional storytelling that has become a defining part of her music. Bruno Mars proves once again why he's one of pop music's most versatile vocalists. His smooth delivery blends naturally with Karol G's softer, more restrained performance, creating a duet built around emotion instead of flashy production. The two artists trade verses before joining together on a soaring chorus that reflects on the difficulty of letting go after a relationship ends. The collaboration also represents one of the most anticipated features on Karol G's latest album, which includes other high-profile guest appearances. No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto takes a noticeably different direction from Karol G's previous projects. Instead of focusing on celebration and empowerment, the album explores heartbreak, grief, acceptance, and personal healing. Throughout the record, Karol G embraces a more reflective sound, with "Still" serving as one of its emotional highlights. It is too early to know how "Still" will perform commercially, but the pairing of Karol G and Bruno Mars gives the song significant global appeal. Their combined fan bases, along with the track's emotional storytelling and English-language lyrics, position it as one of the album's most accessible songs for international audiences. © ¡HOLA! title: Colombian DJ and his husband detained by ICE before embarking on a tour tied to Karol G’s concerts - EL PAÍS English
content: Authorities claim that both individuals have been in the United States on visas that expired in 2022, while their defense team asserts that they have pending asylum cases and valid work permits Everything was set for DJ Tunjo to embark on a U.S. tour hosting unofficial after-parties following concerts by fellow Colombian, superstar Karol G. But the tour ended before it even began. Omar David Panqueva, professionally known as DJ Tunjo, and his husband, Santiago Páez, were arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents after arriving at Chicago Midway Airport to board a flight to Washington, D.C., the first stop of the tour. The arrests have sparked concern among family members, colleagues, and Chicago’s Latino arts community. According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the couple was arrested for remaining in the United States after their tourist visas expired. The agency said the visas lapsed in 2022, leading to their placement in immigration custody. They were later transferred to a detention facility in Indiana. However, the couple’s legal team argues that both men applied for asylum within the time frame required by law and that their cases remain pending. Their attorney, Enrique Espinoza, said Panqueva and Páez have valid work permits and Social Security numbers and have complied with every requirement imposed by immigration authorities while their asylum applications are being processed. The arrests abruptly halted what was expected to be a major milestone in DJ Tunjo’s career. The Colombian artist had planned to travel across several U.S. cities hosting after-parties following Karol G’s concerts, a project he had announced weeks earlier as one of the biggest opportunities of his professional life. In recent months, Panqueva had become an increasingly recognizable figure in Chicago’s Latino music scene. He performed at the Sueños Music Festival in May and later appeared at other events across the city, establishing himself as one of the promoters of spaces dedicated to Latin American music and culture. Family members told Block Club Chicago that the couple moved to Chicago in 2021 and have since focused on projects aimed at bringing together the Latino community through music. In addition to DJ Tunjo’s performances, they organized initiatives supporting emerging artists and creating cultural events. Santiago Páez’s sister said the couple left Colombia because they faced persecution as members of the LGBTQ+ community, prompting them to seek asylum in the United States. The family has also expressed concern that the spouses remain separated inside the detention facility while awaiting developments in their immigration cases. The legal process is ongoing. According to immigration records cited by multiple news outlets, Páez is scheduled to appear before an immigration judge on August 19, while the couple’s legal team is seeking to keep them together and allow them to continue pursuing their asylum case. Following news of the arrests, music promoters, artists, and supporters launched a fundraising campaign to help cover the couple’s legal expenses. The effort has raised thousands of dollars and received strong backing from members of Chicago’s arts community, who credit DJ Tunjo with promoting Latino culture and creating welcoming spaces for immigrants. The case comes amid reports of an increase in immigration arrests at U.S. airports. Various reports indicate that immigration authorities have stepped up the detention of people with expired visas, even when they have active immigration proceedings pending. The increase coincides with expanded cooperation between the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and ICE to share information about non-U.S. citizen travelers following an information-sharing agreement signed by the two agencies in 2025. title: Did You Catch These Easter Eggs in Karol G’s ‘No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto’? - Remezcla
content: In her new album, La Bichota is letting her guard down and she’s in her feelings. Karol G lives up to the title of her LP No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, where she allows herself to get carried away by all the emotions of a breakup. We’re breaking down all the Easter eggs on the very personal album, including lyrics that may relate to her recent heartbreak, collaborators like Bruno Mars and Drake, and poignant samples. At the top of the year, news broke that Karol G and fellow Colombian singer Feid ended their relationship. In his Feid Vs Ferxxo EP, he appeared to touch on the split in the songs “Que vuelta vox” and “Boleritoxx.” Though Karol G hasn’t confirmed who the subject of No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto is, she now appears to be having her say. The album opens with the defiant “Te Llevas To,” in which Karol G addresses a “cabrón.” In Spanish, she sings lyrics like “I felt like I lost by putting you first” and “you took everything except my dignity.” Karol G opens up more in “Maybe,” where she sings, “We tried to fly together, but we couldn’t reach the sky.” She later whispers, “I don’t know if those were good times or if there’s better ones on the way.” It’s no secret that Karol G is a fan of Britney Spears. She previously paid tribute to the pop princess’ “I’m a Slave 4 U” in the “Gatúbela” music video. Now, the blue album cover for No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto has also drawn comparisons to Spears’ Britney and In the Zone eras. Karol G blends the early Euro-pop sound of Spears with reggaeton in “Bebiendo Lágrimas.” She sings about partying the pain away by drinking her tears. Karol G slyly adds, “I’m going to roll myself a blunt with your promises.” The singer then appears to have her “Everytime” moment in the Oklou-produced “Final Feliz”, where she sings, “Hug me again / Come back to me.” Last week, Drake showed up to Karol G’s concert in Toronto. Rumors quickly swirled that she might be romantically involved with the Canadian rapper. Though they’re probably just collaborators, their song “Ahí” appears to play around with the gossip, with Drake singing fully in Spanish. Backed by Afrobeats with atmospheric R&B, Karol G reveals that she’s not ready for romance while recovering from heartbreak. Drake reassures her with the line: “Calm down, you have me here / I’ll wait for my moment.” Another big surprise on the album is Karol G singing fully in English with Bruno Mars. “Still” is a dreamy pop-rock song that’s slightly reminiscent of Keane’s “Somewhere Only We Know.” La Bichota digs deep vocally to match the power of Mars’ voice as they belt together: “I still love you even with a broken heart.” An interesting sample on the album is Jeanette’s “Porque Te Vas” that Karol G morphs into sad perreo in “Con Quién Andará?” Her song with Spanish acts Rusowsky and Judeline, “bbY Wow,” has a dancehall beat that’s similar to Kat DeLuna’s “Whine Up” and Nina Sky’s “Move Ya Body.” Karol G is also a big Selena fan. Following her tribute to the late Mexican-American icon with “Mi Ex Tenía Razón,” she taps into the Tejano music sound once again for the colorful “Alguien Que Te Amaba.” She even references a wilted flower like in Selena’s classic “Como La Flor.” While Karol G’s Mañana Será Bonito album was about healing from a breakup, she simply allows herself to feel everything in No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto with no regrets. title: The Meaning Behind Every Song on Karol G’s Most Personal Album, In Her Own Words - Rolling Stone
content: It’s Tuesday afternoon, and Karol G just landed in Las Vegas, where she’s getting ready for a massive show at the Allegiant Stadium. She’s on a Zoom call from her hotel room, bubbly, ebullient, and excited as ever. Part of this is because a ton is happening: She’s in the middle of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, which is taking on a wild ride across the globe. If that weren’t enough, she’s releasing No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, an album that shocked fans when she surprise-announced it this month. She’s practically radiating as she talks about how excited she is to share it with the world. But huge news aside, that constantly upbeat, vivacious personality is just who Karol is. Yet she’s not afraid to admit that last year, she felt a little like a different person. She’d had a packed couple of years: She’d released Tropicoqueta, she made history as the first Latina to headline Coachella, and she’d played stages from Crazy Horse in Paris to the Vatican. Yet behind the scenes, she was going through a lot, including a highly public break-up, family drama, and tons of criticism around her album. She needed a break. “In the midst of everything, I canceled a lot of things with the team. I told them during Latin Grammys week, ’I need to stop.’ I had never spoken to them so honestly before, but I told them that I had a lot of chaos in my head, a lot of chaos in my heart, that I needed to pause,” she says. “The very next day after the Latin Grammys, I went to Hawaii and I lived there for about a month and two weeks.” The Colombian star, who is usually the bright center of every party, wanted to be alone. She was completely by herself and sat in her room, constantly writing. “I kept myself busy with my notebooks, and I wrote a lot of lyrics, poems, and things,” she remembers. “I didn’t feel like this was going to be like an album, but I did start writing a lot of music because, like, as an artist and as a composer, you really experience a lot of catharsis through music.” She built a little insular world, listening to her favorite band Cigarettes After Sex, plus the Marias, Latin Mafia, and Oklou. But she still didn’t feel right. “I don’t know myself. It’s like I’m a different person. I’ve become super cold. I didn’t want to talk to my friends, I didn’t want to talk to anyone,” Karol remembers thinking. The only thing that helped were letters from fans her team would bring her. Reading what they’d written her gave the singer motivation to talk about what she was feeling, and soon, she was back in the studio, with an outpouring of feelings. The result ended up being No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, Karol’s most vulnerable, emotional album yet. It’s also a wayfaring, experimental mix of pop sounds, bouncing between electronic production, aching balladry, and huge star-studded swings. She teams up with Drake, Bruno Mars, Judeline, Rusowsky, and more, creating an intimate portrait of heartbreak intended for fans to listen to from beginning to end. With her producers, who include longtime collaborators Ovy on the Drums, Sky Rompiendo, Edgar Barrera, and Tainy, she refines the tender-hearted sounds on the album (Oklou, who she kept listening to throughout the process, joins on one song.) The album, Karol admits, was finished for months, but she wanted to wait for the right time to share it. “This album has been ready for a long time, but to be honest, I didn’t want it to feel like I was exploiting a personal situation. I didn’t want it to feel like this album was part of some marketing campaign. It was very personal to me. It was so personal that I didn’t even feel ready to release it,” she says. However, now that she’s found catharsis —  and constant warmth from her fans on her tour every night, she decided it felt like the right time. “The reason I decided to put the record outside is simply so that people let themselves feel,” Karol says. “The point of this album is for people to understand that to truly live, we have to feel. If we limit ourselves and let ourselves go, ‘I don’t want to feel, I’m not going to fall in love, I’m not going to give myself the chance, I’m not going to speak up, I’m not going to say anything,’ then we’re not going to live. Living is about feeling — feeling things, feeling every moment, and feeling it to the fullest.” Below, she breaks down all the songs on the album and shares how the music helped her heal and ultimately find herself again. “Te Llevas To'”This song is a mix of things. I kept telling Tainy, “This has to sound chaotic,” because the emotion I was feeling was anger that comes from chaos. I was in my head like, “I need to get out what I want to say, and I feel like the production has to sound like chaos.” We started with the person in the song looking back, and everything is over: There’s no faith, no future, nothing. Everything has happened. But then it says, “Let me tell you all the good things I’m left with, even though you broke this.” We started with a synthesizer and then we went to these intense drums which are super chaotic. By the end, you just exhale. You’re like, “I let it out.” And that song was the perfect one to start with. “Maybe”The second track was putting things into context a little more and explaining what was happening. In the first one, I vented my anger. In the second, it’s almost like I’m telling a story through the songs, and that’s when we get to “Maybe.” In “Maybe,” I wanted to start with that phrase, “This time I’m not going to lose you,” which is a phrase that’s repeated a million times in relationships on the brink and it’s never realistic. Like, the relationship gets more and more broken each time, but you’re like, “This time, yes, this time yes, it’ll work.” But in the end, it’s like when you can’t take it anymore, you just can’t. It was super important for me to start the song with that lyric. “Maybe” explains a little bit like, “We couldn’t build anything more here.” “Bebiendo Lágrimas”“Bebiendo Lagrimas” is when you tell yourself, “I don’t want to go through that again, never again. Love is over.” I said in the trailer I released a few days ago, sometimes you just stop believing in everything. Why? Because pain, specifically, makes you doubt everything, like empathy or kindness in life. I feel like in life, it’s not just one situation. Life changes you little by little, little by little. As humans, we see that people, for some reason, change or give off a different kind of energy, and we sometimes don’t ask ourselves what’s happening to them, what they’re going through, and what we could do for that person to make them feel different. What we do instead is to punish them. So the message of that song is, “I’ve reached my limit in matters of love. I’m burying it, and at least for now, I’m going to enjoy my peace, myself, being alone, enjoying who I am — my career, my friends. But at the moment, I have locked it all away, I’m peaceful, and I prefer it that way. I prefer to be like this.” That’s what I was telling myself. This was one of the first tracks for the album, if not the first. “Ahí” (feat. Drake)This is like when you’re no longer in a relationship and you can meet people. But you have to give yourself the space to recover, give yourself time. So, it’s the feeling of saying, “Thank you, you’re an amazing person. I’m probably denying myself the chance to experience something amazing, but for now, I can’t. But I’ll keep it there in case it happens in the future.” I wrote that song on Dec. 31. I didn’t celebrate Christmas partying and all that, but I went to a place in Colombia called Guatapé, and it was more of a retreat. [My producer] Ovy came with me. He went with his family, and I was with mine. Drake singing in Spanish has always been incredible to me; it never seems forced, and I’d had an interaction with him before. He’d written to me once on Instagram to ask me to send a video to his masseuse who was a huge fan so I sent it and then we kept talking about how cool it would be to do something together. But that was a long time ago so when this song happened, I had that conversation in mind. We started talking about making it a duet, like the verses responding to each other. And I was like, “I don’t know, but I’d love it if Drake sang it in Spanish.” The first week of January, we sent him the song and he loved it. By like January 8, he was in the Bahamas making Iceman and our teams met up for like three days to work out the track. I guided him through the recording so I could help him with the pronunciation. It was literally just him, his engineer, and me in the studio. There was no one else. I was with him in the booth, like, “You have to say it more like this. You have to say it.” The pronunciation was super important to him, and he was constantly like, “Please, I have to get the pronunciation down.” I feel like it turned out amazing. A little bit of the song leaked, so people were like, “Karol G is on Iceman,” and in one of his songs he mentions me. I think that people have been waiting for this collaboration. “Final Feliz”Oklou did the production, but originally, it was just a song on guitar. I wrote it with Judeline and it was all acoustic. But Oklou’s stimulates my brain, my emotions, and she uses a lot of ambient sounds, very much in keeping with her production style. It sounds very fresh, very distinct. I told my sister, “I have this song and I feel like what I’m imagining for the production could be done by her.” Plus, I admire her because she just became a mom, she’s on tour, she inspires me so much. “Final Feliz” is a song that talks about when you decide to leave someone because you know where things are headed. And it’s the hardest moment when you decide to leave because you’re not going to wait for the harder blow later. So you’re like “This can’t go on. It’s going to go badly, badly, badly, badly.” It’s that pain of someone you really want, but it just can’t happen. It’s that duality.  “It could have been a happy ending, but it wasn’t.” When I submitted the song to Oklou, she immediately asked for my personal number. She wrote to me like, “Wow. I have to be honest, I was surprised because I haven’t heard this side of you before, and I’m so excited to be a part of it.” It’s one of my favorite songs on the album. She made it special and it still resonates with me. “Still” (feat. Bruno Mars)I’ve always had it in mind to make music in English, but it’s something I’ve never pushed for, and this song found me. I’m really excited about the idea of a song like this in English, not because I want to change who I am, but because I also have so many fans whose first language is English, and one day I wanted to be able to speak to them from that perspective. When the composers Isabel and Tomás [LaRosa] sent me this song, I felt something very strange. It was as if someone had written exactly what I was going through. We tried to imagine it in other ways, but the truth is, I never felt that anything needed to be changed. The song already had a soul, and I couldn’t stop listening to it and feeling it that way. Then we sent it to Bruno. He connected with it just as strongly and decided to be a part of it. We changed some things in the lyrics a bit, and he also participated in the production. The beautiful thing is that it was never conceived with a market in mind. This album is about letting go of your feelings. And this song was exactly that. Instead of translating it or adapting it to fit, I decided to respect it just as it came to me. Honestly, having a song with Bruno is something I still can’t believe. In fact, yesterday we were here in Las Vegas, and we were hanging out because we were making some content we’re going to be sharing for the song, and I have to be honest, it feels super surreal. I traveled to where he was to record because he was on tour, and it was like a whirlwind trip I had to make in one go so I could finish the song quickly and have it ready. I traveled, spent two days with him, and he directed my recording in the studio, it was just his engineer, my engineer, him, and me again. There was no one else there, and he was kind of directing my vocal delivery, my pronunciation. He was like, “I want you to keep your accent, but I’m going to make sure that what’s said is understood.” We were in the studio from 7:00 PM until 9:00 AM the next day. I’m super open to [music in English]. The only thing I wouldn’t do is sit down and try to do a whole album in English like, “This is my English album.” But it’s about the right song. I feel like what happened with this song is that I really fell in love with it, and I really wanted to include a song in English on my album where I was speaking to a specific audience. If I had the opportunity to connect differently, like, now that we’re going to Coachella and you start to see that there’s a new audience and  might not speak Spanish at all. “Alguien Que Te Amaba”I ended up working on this song with Pete Astudillo, the composer of Selena Quintanilla’s songs. I was like, “Wow, I would love to work with that person.” Since she passed away, he never really worked with anyone else. And it was super crazy because I was with Edgar, and I said, “It would be a dream to work with him.” Edgar was like, “He hasn’t made music in a long time but let’s look for him and see what happens.” Then he tracked him down and said, “He super into it,” and it meant so much because he listened to my album from the heart. Something that Trópicoqueta gave me, which is huge, was identity. From the beginning of my career I’ve always made it very clear that I’m Colombian, I’m Latina, and on the stages I’ve performed on, I’ve always tried to make that very clear, but with Trópicoqueta, it was like the world understood it. And in fact, it was an album that I feel made more people who didn’t speak Spanish understand who Karol G is. With No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, even though I was very clear that I wanted a more intimate, alternative, sound, I didn’t want to stray too far from the Latin sounds that say, “Wow! It’s Karol G.” “Matadora” We all knew what could happen when “Matadora” came out, obviously because of the themes of the song and the way I’m expressing myself on it. But I do feel like “Karol G is always going to surprise you.” So I wanted it to be the first song people heard on this album because it’s like a movie that starts with the final scene. And this is how I feel now — I didn’t feel like this a few months ago. Now I feel “Matadora,” but obviously like a normal human, I have good days, I have not so good days, but I feel like I’m at a point of clarity and lucidity, where I want to live peacefully, where I want to keep fulfilling my dreams, where I want to keep having the opportunity to connect, where I want to go out, do things with my friends. That’s how I feel today, like that song. Since we’re in the public eye and the media is so focused on artists all the time, we knew what was going to happen in the press, but I actually feel like the song connected better than we thought. It’s growing more and more on streaming every day. People are starting to use it. I’ve seen videos of girls all dressed up, getting ready, in their swimsuits. I just love having songs that embrace female sensuality, especially because that has been so suppressed and frowned upon. I love being able to put those songs out there, where women feel beautiful, gorgeous, powerful. I love this song and putting it out first made people go, “Wait, ‘Matadora,’ but the album is called ‘I don’t regret feeling so much?” I think it made people excited about what else is coming on the album. “For You My Love”Everyone on my team loves this song. To be honest, that song was the hardest for me to place on the tracklist. The tracklist is super important to me because it’s the experience the fan will have when they listen to the whole album, beginning to end, and that song, because of its sound, didn’t quite fit anywhere. But I felt it was important because it symbolizes when you reach a point where you start to see everything that happened to you from a different emotional perspective. And it’s not so much about the pain anymore, but rather that time has passed, you’ve understood it, you’ve moved on. And when you remember that person, you’re like, ”Aw, that was so great,” and you see it from a more positive perspective. So the sound of the song was more positive. And I felt it had to be on the tracklist because it’s part of the process. I thought about making it the third song, or leaving it for last, because in the emotional process it would be the last step. But I wanted to add a boost here and then you get back to the emotion. I made that with Edgar too, and I’m telling you, when we made it in the studio, there was this incredible magic in the room. I wanted it to start with an organ, which could be a wedding or a funeral, so that duality was also a big part of it. And I can’t wait for people to see the video. “Si Lo Ven”I could say this song is like the soul of the album. I decided to sing it at my last show. For me, that song, literally, every bar, every bit of it is the soul of the album. It’s what I was just saying, simply allowing yourself to feel and saying it, not like, “Oh, look at me be strong or like I don’t care.” No. This was the spirit of the album and that’s where I decided, it’s not about being strong or preserving. I want people to finish this album with the initial emotion. I wanted to do that for several reasons. One, I don’t feel like I’m fully OK yet. I’m not saying I’m not doing well, but I feel like the fact that I’m not ready to experience my life with anyone or open myself up to new experiences makes me feel like I’m still in the healing process, if you know what I mean. I’m still in a process. So it couldn’t end on a different note because I’m not exactly there yet. “Bby Wow” (feat. Judeline and Rusowsky)I felt like I needed a song, one that people could dance to in the club but that also had that emotion. So, what happens when you’re in the club and you’re heartbroken? You just think about the other person, about the song you’d love to be dancing to with that person. The first version of the song was just me. But I felt like, live, I wanted to sing that song with more people on stage and for it to really become a bit more of a party. And that’s when I thought of Rusowsky and I said to Judeline, “Why don’t you join the song?” I worked a lot on that album with Judeline because the way she sings about love made me feel how men sometimes don’t understand how deep a woman’s pain can be. She has something special, and it’s that every emotion feels so intense. She has a song called “Is God Good or Just Powerful?” It’s literally one that lasts about a minute and a half. What she sings is super short, it’s like a verse and a chorus. And I was like, “Wow, how can you say so much in a verse and a chorus?” So it was literally a must for me to write music with her for this album. Our teams got in touch. We told her I was making new music and she traveled to Los Angeles. I spent about a week with her, and it was really nice because the first thing we did was sit down and talk, like, “I’ll give you some context about where I am, how I’m feeling.”We were both going through almost the same thing, so I loved that because we were in sync and it just worked. I thought, “We’re both here, feeling almost the same thing, it’s going to flow in a special way.”We were in the studio for about three or four days, and we made more music there that isn’t on the album. “Con Quién Andará?”“Con Quién Andará?” is another core of the album because it’s you in your room, asking yourselves five thousand questions: “What’s happening with that other person? What are they doing?” And that’s something you ask yourself every day, for a long time, many hours of your day. So, “Con Quién Andará?” is a core song that gets at the feelings of the album. I want people, when they finish the album, listening in bed, staring at the ceiling and all, to leave them with the emotion I had all that time. I feel like sometimes they tell you, “No, but don’t let it get to you and listen to those songs.” No, that’s the best part of heartbreak, it’s not going to bed and letting the music speak for you. One of the things I’m excited about is seeing my fans live. Being able to experience the album live with all my fans while I’m still on tour is going to be like a community, like everyone is feeling included. I feel like I’m going to start seeing those who will arrive dressed in orange for Tropicoqueta or those who will arrive dressed in blue. So I’m really excited because I feel like my concert is going to be like that movie In and Out. (laughs.) We’re adding a while section to the show, so I can’t wait for people to see it. “Eclipse”“Eclipse” was the song I was going to end the album with because at the end, I don’t know if you hear it, but it says, “God, take care of him for me because I’m going to let him go.” This is sort of that moment of looking and saying, “It didn’t work but why was it so special and so beautiful? But I’m ready to let go.” Honestly, with the album about to come out, I’m super happy. I feel like I’ve already made peace with a lot of things that are sure to start happening after the album. But I’m absolutely certain, based on the letters from all my fans and the personal things they write to me — because they write very personal things in their letters, like very specific situations they’re going through — I know that if this album reaches someone, it’s going to reach the right person, and that makes me feel purposeful. If they understand me, it simply makes me feel that everything I’ve experienced had a reason. And being able to experience it live with all my fans it is going to be like a community. “Después de Ti”This song is beyond just emotion. It’s when you feel like you’re ungrounded. Things happen, and I’m talking about life in different situations, not just in love, but when you’re in a situation where you’re left not knowing what to do, where to turn, what to do with your life, what to do with what you’re feeling. You’re suspended, while everything in life passes by and it’s like your life isn’t passing, like time is passing but you’re not living it. It’s like being on an airplane that’s in the air but isn’t moving. That’s “Después de Ti.” It’s like, “After you, this is me now. I don’t know what to do, I don’t know what to say, I don’t know how to speak, I don’t know how to express myself, I don’t know anything anymore.” And I ended things with her because people had already heard it, and I feel like when it ended with “Eclipse,” this song kind of reinforced the feeling emotionally. So putting it there, it was more about feeling. I don’t know if it fits in the story’s order, but that was the exact feeling I wanted people to end up with. The fact that my life is so exposed is incredibly complex for me. But it’s also taught me that what matters is what I think of myself, not what other people think of me. I believe you can save yourself from what everyone else thinks of you, but you can’t save yourself from what you think of yourself. So, these past months have been about working on myself, on my personal growth. I feel like I’ve reached a point where I’m working incredibly hard, I’m incredibly disciplined, and I’m connected with my friends and my family. Then I go on stage and I meet all these people who have a real, normal life like mine, who actually understand everything I’m going through. And I think, “This is what it’s all about.” So, honestly, today I feel really good, yesterday, these past few days, this week. It won’t always be like this. I always say that happiness isn’t a constant state, but rather like sparks, moments, but being at peace is different, and I feel at peace. I feel at peace with myself, with my life, with my story, with what’s happening around me. So I’m totally ready to show it to the world. We want to hear it. Send us a tip using our anonymous form. title: Karol G’s New Album ‘No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto’ Featuring Drake & More Is Here: Stream It Now - Billboard
content:
The 14-track album follows 2025'sTropicoqueta, which debuted at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums. Karol G’s sixth studio album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, arrived on Friday (Aug. 7). On the tracklist revealed Wednesday (Aug. 5), the artist surprised fans with star-studded collaborators Drake on “Ahí,” Bruno Mars on “Still” and Judeline and Rusowsky on “Bby Wow.” The 14-track set is also home to the previously released singles “Después de Ti” with Cigarettes After Sex guitarist Greg Gonzalez and “Matadora,” which debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Latin Songs chart on the tally dated Aug. 8, 2026. Karol premiered the former during her first headlining weekend at Coachella in April, and the latter during the kickoff of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour on July 24 in Chicago’s Soldier Field. A follow-up to her 2025 Tropicoqueta album that debuted at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums and No. 3 on the all-genre Billboard 200, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto (which translates to “I Don’t Regret Feeling So Much”), moves away from the prior vibrant and tropical-leaning album, and demonstrates a more intimate, stripped-down look at the artist born Carolina Giraldo Navarro. “In my room, I have a ritual: I put up little lights, I burn candles and incense. I want people to listen to this new album that’s coming, in their own rooms, and see what comes up for them,” she said in an interview with Elle in which she discussed her new album. “I’d rather suffer because I lived too much — because I loved too much, because I had too much fun — than to not have had those experiences, you know? I’m inviting everyone to be a little more dramatic, a little more extra.” The “Bichota” singer teased a new album was dropping during her concert at Rogers Stadium in Toronto on July 29. “I’ve been working on a project for a couple of months,” she told onlookers. “I’ve been locked in for months making new music. For months, I’ve been preparing a segment that will form part of this tour.” Your email address will not be published.
